Show HN: Tori by TalkJS. AI support that's actually good
item.description:
Hey everyone!

Joshua and Egbert from TalkJS here. Today we're launching Tori, an AI support agent built for difficult product questions.

Other tools we tried struggled with the technical questions we get at TalkJS, so we built our own. One of our test questions was: "How can I add two-way sync between TalkJS and my Minecraft mod?"

Our docs never mention Minecraft, and TalkJS does not have a Java SDK. Tori figured out how a Java Edition mod could use Kotlin, found our Kotlin Data API even though it isn't mentioned on the homepage, and explained step-by-step how to connect the two. It avoided the obvious solution of REST + webhooks, and explained why that would be insecure in a clientside mod.

That's what it means for support to actually be good. Understand what customers are trying to build, research the features and limitations, and work out how they fit together. Tori works great even when no single page contains the answer.

Tori browses your live website and documentation, no retraining step. We've been using it for TalkJS support over the past few months, and it handles 87% of our customer enquiries autonomously.

Customers can ask for a human at any point, and you can always see what Tori is telling them and what it thinks. So your team can jump in and work alongside Tori, with the conversation and research already there. Our goal is for your customers to get good help faster, with human support always in reach.

Tori is built on TalkJS, whose infrastructure handles 130M+ monthly messages. The TalkJS base means you can fully customize the interface's components, layout and behavior to fit your product.

You also get direct access to senior Tori developers for free, including help with customization. We're launching early so customers can help shape the product.

Have a go at https://asktori.ai. We're curious what you think!

Ask HN: How to organize teams to ship AI-written code?
item.description:
Inspired by the discussion in [1], I have an adjacent question: did your team organization and work methods change?

In our company we still try to play by the (old) book: backlogs, estimates, iterations, feature teams, PR reviews, etc., but the entire thing leaks everywhere you look. There is no point in many of the old rituals, but it is also not clear how to organize ourselves now. This is different, albeit closely related, from the question of how to adjust as an IC.

For example:

- In our team, we almost don't see the point in PR reviews anymore, not in the old way anyway. Generated code is always good enough, and in a sense is already reviewed once by the developer who signed off (the topic is discussed in [1]). So, we are now thinking to abandon PRs, or change what we review and how we do it. We are adding more rules for code review agents and to CI. We are also thinking to replace code reviews by "concept reviews" or similar.

- Speaking of those, we still try to find the right place and a process for architecture and specifications reviews. They seem to become a new subject of PR reviews in fact, but we are not there yet.

- In many places we don't see the need to share the workload and knowledge between multiple developers. Reverting to the model where one developer is responsible for an entire component seems viable again. Although we are naturally worried about BusFactor=1.

- Some Agile-inspired practices still work for us, namely iterative development and "deploy when ready". But the development process itself starts to resemble the old-school waterfall-ish one: think everything through, write down your constraints and your specs, design the architecture first, then (re)generate the code at will. I wonder what other practices will go away or get adopted.

There are probably more examples, hopefully you get the gist. I am very interested in discussing how do we organize the teams now? What did you try? What works, what doesn't?

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50151036 (Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?)

Show HN: Pando, an open-source platform to deploy and share apps built with AI
item.description:
Hey all! As the use of AI continues to grow and becomes more available to less technical users, I feel that “Shadow AI” is starting to become a problem, since users are building apps with AI, but there’s nowhere to put them, and no way to share them. I have seen this firsthand while working in the IT and DevOps space since before generative AI was a thing.

So, I started building Pando! It’s an open source platform that you can run yourself, and it allows users to deploy apps build with AI easily, and share them with others in your org (or family). It scans each app for known vulnerabilities, and runs them in isolated networks.

It’s still very much in alpha, but I would love some people to give it a try and provide feedback on the project and its direction!
